claim: Claude Opus 5.5 defaults to effort `medium` where Claude Opus 5 defaulted to `high`, so a request or setup that omits effort now runs one level lower than before.
why: The source tells integrators to set effort explicitly and re-run their sweep instead of carrying over the Claude Opus 5 setting.
check: Look for Opus 5.5 subagents, skills or settings that leave effort unset while relying on Opus 5 `high` behavior; flag unset effort as an unmeasured choice.
quote: Start at `medium`, the default on Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Opus 5 defaults to `high`), set it explicitly, and test several levels against your own evals

claim: Effort level names do not mean the same amount of thinking across models: Opus 5.5 at `medium` matches or beats Opus 5 at `high` on coding and knowledge-work evals, and `low` often comes close at much lower cost.
why: The source reports this from Anthropic testing and warns against mapping levels one-to-one.
check: When advising a move from Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, check whether an old `high` or `xhigh` setting was copied over; suggest sweeping `low` and `medium` first.
quote: Effort level names don’t correspond to the same amount of thinking across models: in Anthropic’s testing, Claude Opus 5.5 at `medium` matches or exceeds Claude Opus 5 at `high` on coding and knowledge-work evaluations

claim: At the same effort level Opus 5.5 tends to think more per turn than Opus 5, most of all at `xhigh` and `max`, so carried-over settings produce longer turns and more output tokens.
why: Higher thinking per turn raises cost, latency and the chance of cut-off replies.
check: Flag Opus 5.5 setups that run `xhigh` or `max` by default without a measured quality gain.
quote: At a given level, Claude Opus 5.5 tends to think more per turn than Claude Opus 5, especially at `xhigh` and `max`.

claim: To make Opus 5.5 think less, lower the effort level before adding prompt instructions to think less.
why: Lowering effort reduces thinking, cost and latency more reliably than prompt wording does.
check: Look in Opus 5.5 instruction files for lines like 'don't overthink' or 'think briefly' used in place of a lower effort setting.
quote: Lowering effort reduces thinking, and with it cost and latency, more reliably than prompt instructions do.

claim: On Opus 5.5 thinking is always on: `thinking: {type: disabled}` and manual `budget_tokens` both return a 400 at every effort level, and effort is the only control over thinking depth.
why: Opus 5 accepted `disabled` at effort `high` or below; Opus 5.5 removed that option.
check: Search Agent SDK apps, subagent configs and scripts targeting Opus 5.5 for `disabled` thinking or `budget_tokens`; each one will fail.
quote: On Claude Opus 5.5, thinking is always on: a request that sets

claim: For a route that ran Opus 5 with thinking disabled, the source suggests starting at `low` effort, optionally adding the line 'Answer directly without deliberating.', and measuring quality because less thinking can lower it.
why: At `low` the model keeps thinking short, and how often it skips thinking depends on the prompts.
check: If an Opus 5.5 setup needs fast first tokens, check that it uses `low` effort and has measured quality, not just a prompt line.
quote: a system prompt line such as “Answer directly without deliberating.” can reduce thinking further; measure quality when you add it, because less thinking can lower it.

claim: Instructions that ask Opus 5.5 to write its reasoning into the reply as a substitute for thinking should be removed, because such prompts can be declined with the `reasoning_extraction` refusal category; read reasoning from summarized thinking blocks instead.
why: The classifier treats pushing the model to reproduce its internal reasoning in response text as a violation.
check: Grep instruction files and system prompts for 'show your reasoning step by step in the answer' style rules aimed at Opus 5.5 and flag them.
quote: A prompt that pushes the model to reproduce its reasoning in the response text might be declined with the `reasoning_extraction`

claim: Any rule telling Opus 5.5 not to think should be removed regardless, since thinking is always on; the thinking-disabled mitigation instructions from Opus 5 should be re-tested rather than kept by default.
why: Those mitigations addressed artifacts that appeared on Opus 5 only when thinking was disabled.
check: Flag 'do not think' or 'respond without reasoning' rules and the Opus 5 combined tool-call/no-XML-tags mitigation in Opus 5.5 setups.
quote: With thinking always on, check whether you still need the instruction, and remove the no-thinking rule either way.

claim: On long multipart tasks Opus 5.5 posts updates and some of them end the turn with text and no tool call (`stop_reason: end_turn`), so an unattended agent loop that treats any text-only end of turn as completion will stop early.
why: The source says to treat such a turn as a report, not proof the task is done.
check: In loops, stop hooks or harness code driving Opus 5.5, check that completion is judged against a checklist or condition and not by the absence of a tool call.
quote: Treat a text-only end of turn as a report rather than as proof the task is done.

claim: For unattended Opus 5.5 loops, if a turn ends with open checklist items and no stated blocker, send a short user message naming them, and cap automatic continuations at two or three per task so a genuinely stuck run ends.
why: Unbounded continuation would loop forever on a stuck task.
check: Check that any auto-continue mechanism (hook or harness) has a retry cap and names the open items.
quote: stop after two or three automatic continuations on the same task rather than repeating them indefinitely

claim: For fully unattended Opus 5.5 agents the source supplies a standing-instruction paragraph for the end of the system prompt that names four early-stop patterns (summary announcing next step, offer to continue, decision list that blocks nothing, deciding it is a good place to report) and keeps stops where nothing can move without the user.
why: Opus 5.5 responds to instructions that name the specific kinds of early stop to avoid.
check: For unattended Opus 5.5 setups that stall mid-task, check whether a similar named-stop instruction exists; for interactive setups, check it is absent.
quote: A message with no tool call in it ends your turn, and the work stops there until you are asked to continue.

claim: The unattended-agent addition should be added from the first request of a session, kept out of human-in-the-loop applications, and paired with your own confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions; expect somewhat more tool calls and output tokens.
why: Adding it mid-session edits the system prompt and invalidates earlier thinking blocks, and the addition makes the model carry on where it would have checked in.
check: Check that the early-stop addition is not injected mid-conversation and not present in interactive setups where a human answers.
quote: leave the addition out of human-in-the-loop applications, where someone is there to answer.

claim: On Opus 5.5 the short notes written between tool calls come back as progress-update `thinking` blocks with empty text at the default display, so a client rendering only `text` blocks looks silent during a long agentic turn.
why: Opus 5 returned these notes as `text` blocks; Opus 5.5 does not, and no error is raised.
check: For Agent SDK apps or custom UIs on Opus 5.5, check that `thinking.display` is set to `updates` or `summarized` and that non-empty thinking blocks are rendered.
quote: a client that renders only `text` blocks can look silent during a long agentic turn.

claim: If Opus 5.5 turns still go quiet, the harness can count consecutive tool steps with no user-readable text and after about five append the reminder 'The user hasn't heard from you in a while: say in a few words what you're doing, then continue.', stopping after two or three reminders.
why: In Anthropic's agentic coding tests this roughly halved tasks with a long silent stretch with no measurable cost change, and appending keeps the cache and thinking blocks valid.
check: Check that any reminder mechanism appends rather than inserting and later deleting text in earlier turns.
quote: The user hasn't heard from you in a while: say in a few words what you're doing, then continue.

claim: For multi-app workflow agents on Opus 5.5, which tends to get to work quickly, one system-prompt sentence telling it to explore broadly across emails, documents, tabs and records before acting made it complete more tasks correctly at both `medium` and `max`, at a small cost in tool calls and tokens.
why: Information the task depends on often sits where the request does not point.
check: For connected-app agents on Opus 5.5, check for an explore-first instruction, and that untrusted content is kept out of the records it searches.
quote: Before taking any action, explore broadly with tool calls: list and open the emails, documents, spreadsheet tabs, and records across the available apps that could be relevant to this task

claim: In multi-agent setups with Opus 5.5, appending an elapsed-versus-budget line such as `elapsed 340s / 1200s` to each message, or a sentence stressing that time matters, made teams finish sooner; a budget mostly keeps more agents working in parallel, unlike lower effort, which reduces the work.
why: Opus 5.5 is highly responsive to elapsed-time information and paces itself to the budget.
check: For lead-agent and subagent harnesses on Opus 5.5, check whether any time signal is given; for hard limits check that the harness keeps its own timeout.
quote: Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.

claim: An Opus 5.5 time budget is advisory only: nothing stops the model at the limit, and under time pressure it may search and verify a little less.
why: The budget is a prompt signal, not an enforced cutoff.
check: If a harness relies on an elapsed-time line for cost control, check that it also has a real timeout.
quote: The budget is advisory and nothing stops the model at the limit, so if you need a hard stop, keep your own timeout.

claim: Chat system prompts that tell Opus 5.5 to think carefully before answering should be considered for removal, since the model decides how much to think and effort is the control.
why: In Anthropic's chat testing, removing such a line made replies start sooner with no clear quality decline.
check: Grep chat or persona prompts for 'think step by step' or 'think carefully' lines on Opus 5.5 and flag them.
quote: if your system prompt contains instructions that tell Claude to think carefully before answering, consider removing them for Claude Opus 5.5.

claim: In multi-turn chat Opus 5.5 sometimes re-examines an earlier answer when a new message arrives; a two-sentence addition at the end of the system prompt ('Once you have answered something, treat that answer as done...') cuts this, but may make it less likely to volunteer a correction of its own earlier mistake.
why: The source reduces follow-up thinking and latency and warns to leave it out for long analyses and agentic tasks where later steps reveal earlier errors.
check: If this line is present in an agentic or long-analysis Opus 5.5 setup, flag it.
quote: Once you have answered something, treat that answer as done.

claim: To keep Opus 5.5 from following instructions hidden in text a user pasted, wrap each pasted block in matching opening and closing tags carrying the same app-generated random ID, and add a system-prompt note saying such text may contain instructions the user did not write.
why: The model is robust to injected instructions in pasted content only when it can tell which text is the user's own.
check: For Opus 5.5 apps that accept pasted emails or web content, check the pasted blocks are tagged with a random per-block id and that the system prompt carries the note.
quote: Wrap each pasted block in an opening and a closing tag that both carry the same short random ID, generated by your application, with each tag on its own line:

claim: For Opus 5.5 frontend work, name the specific default patterns to avoid (e.g. cream background, italic accent words, numbered section labels, monospace labels, pill buttons) and extend the list iteratively; a general 'avoid a generic AI look' mostly swaps one default for another.
why: Without design direction the model falls back on a few default styles.
check: In frontend or design skills for Opus 5.5, flag vague style instructions that name no concrete patterns.
quote: It responds well to instructions that name specific patterns to avoid, as in the following example.

claim: Scaffolding built for chart, diagram and screenshot reading on earlier models may be unnecessary on Opus 5.5, which reads them far more precisely without tools; for the densest inputs, higher resolution and crop/zoom/measure tooling in a container still add accuracy.
why: Opus 5.5 at low effort read dense charts better than Opus 5 at its highest effort in Anthropic's testing.
check: For vision pipelines moved to Opus 5.5, check for obsolete workarounds, and for dense technical drawings check that image tools exist.
quote: re-test whether you still need scaffolding you built for visual inputs on earlier models.

claim: Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`) is positioned for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, with agentic coding gains largest on multistep work in a real repository.
why: The source ties the model to this use and reports it matched Opus 5 at `high` while using fewer steps and about half the tokens.
check: Judge whether heavy multistep repository work and long autonomous runs in a setup run on Opus 5.5 rather than a smaller model.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 is built for long-running agentic coding and knowledge work, priced at $4 / $20 USD per million input / output tokens.

claim: Opus 5.5 rejects forced tool use: `tool_choice` of type `any` or `tool` returns a 400 on Messages, Batches and token counting; use `auto` plus `strict: true`, structured outputs, or a prompt saying when the tool applies.
why: Forced tool use is unsupported on this model, as on Fable 5.1.
check: Look for forced `tool_choice` in Agent SDK apps or scripts that target Opus 5.5 and check there is an `auto` plus tool-call-happened check replacement.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 doesn’t support forced tool use.

claim: Opus 5.5 thinking blocks are read only by a few other models, so a router switch, retry or classifier fallback to Opus 5 or Opus 4.8 runs the later turns without Opus 5.5's reasoning; blocks are dropped by the API, not billed, and should be passed back unchanged.
why: Each thinking block records which model produced it.
check: For setups that route or fall back between models mid-conversation, note that reasoning continuity is lost on most switches away from Opus 5.5.
quote: so a router switch, a client-side retry on another model, or a classifier-refusal fallback (server-side or SDK middleware) to Claude Opus 5 / Claude Opus 4.8 runs the turns after the switch without Claude Opus 5.5's reasoning.

claim: The thinking-block prefix check (system prompt, tools and earlier messages must be byte-identical) is enforced by default for accounts created on or after 2026-08-31 and a violating replay returns a 400; Claude Code, claude.ai, Managed Agents and the Agent SDK keep the prefix intact, while code that builds `messages` itself must stay append-only.
why: Editing earlier history invalidates replayed thinking blocks; it also lowers prompt-cache hit rates.
check: For custom harnesses on Opus 5.5, check for per-turn reminders later deleted, mid-session system prompt edits, tool add/remove, or client compaction that replays older thinking blocks.
quote: Claude Code, claude.ai, Managed Agents, and the Agent SDK keep the prefix intact

claim: Opus 5.5 adds a biology safety classifier that Opus 5 lacks, alongside cybersecurity and reasoning-extraction classifiers; refusals arrive as HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: refusal`, and `reasoning_extraction` declines are not retried by server-side fallback.
why: The biology safeguards match Fable 5.1's and decline dual-use biology research such as virology and toxicology.
check: For life-science or security work on Opus 5.5, check that code branches on `stop_reason: refusal` and that a fallback is configured.
quote: The biology safeguards are the same as Claude Fable 5.1’s, and Claude Opus 5 doesn’t have them.

claim: On the Claude API and Google Cloud, Opus 5.5 rejects the `computer_20251124` tool with a 400 and accepts only the `computer_toolset_20260801` toolset (no beta header, no name or display size); Amazon Bedrock still accepts `computer_20251124`.
why: The toolset replaces the earlier tool on those platforms and needs agent-loop changes.
check: Check computer-use tool definitions in apps targeting Opus 5.5 on the Claude API or Google Cloud for the old tool type.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 returns a 400 error for any computer use tool version it doesn’t accept, such as `computer_20251124` on the Claude API.

claim: Opus 5.5 `max_tokens` must cover thinking as well as the reply; the prompting guide cites 128,000 (the model maximum) as working well for long agentic coding turns while the migration guide cites 64K as a starting point.
why: Thinking counts toward `max_tokens` even when its text is not returned, so a limit sized for a no-thinking route cuts replies off; the two Anthropic pages give different figures.
check: Flag small `max_tokens` values on Opus 5.5 routes migrated from thinking-off.
quote: a `max_tokens` of 128,000, the model’s maximum, has worked well in Anthropic’s testing

claim: For Opus 5.5 long agentic coding turns the migration guide gives 64K as a reasonable `max_tokens` starting point, which differs from the 128,000 given in the prompting guide.
why: Sources disagree on the suggested figure; the prompting guide says 128,000 worked well in Anthropic's testing, the migration guide says 64K has worked well.
check: Treat either as acceptable; flag only values too small to hold thinking plus reply.
quote: For long agentic coding turns, 64K has worked well.

claim: Instructions tuned for Opus 5 (verbosity, over-verification and scope prompts) may no longer be needed on Opus 5.5 and should be re-tested on your own evals rather than carried over untouched.
why: The model behaviors those prompts compensated for may have changed.
check: In instruction files migrated from Opus 5 to Opus 5.5, flag legacy behavior-patching blocks that have no eval backing them.
quote: may no longer be needed - keep them as the starting point, then re-test each on your own evals rather than carrying them over untouched.

claim: At `xhigh` and `max` Opus 5.5 turns run longer than on Opus 5, so timeouts, streaming and progress UX should be planned for that, and effort lowered before prompting for brevity.
why: Longer turns follow from the extra thinking at those levels.
check: Check timeouts and non-streaming calls in Opus 5.5 setups that use `xhigh` or `max`.
quote: turns run longer than on Claude Opus 5 - plan timeouts, streaming, and progress UX accordingly

claim: Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, below Opus 5's $5 and $25, with cache reads at $0.20 per million (0.05x input) and batch at half price.
why: The deeper cache-read discount makes keeping the prompt cache warm matter more in long agentic sessions.
check: When comparing model costs for a setup, use these rates rather than Opus 5's, and check that cache-breaking edits are avoided.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 USD per million input tokens and $20 USD per million output tokens, below Claude Opus 5’s $5 and $25 USD

claim: Changing the top-level effort value between requests invalidates the cached messages on Opus 5.5; per-message effort (beta) changes it mid-conversation while keeping the cache.
why: Per-message effort is applied without editing the cached prefix.
check: If a harness switches effort between requests mid-session, flag the cache invalidation and suggest per-message effort.
quote: Changing the top-level `effort` value between requests invalidates the cached messages.

claim: Claude Sonnet 5.5 effort levels are recalibrated relative to Sonnet 5: the API default stays `high` but a level no longer yields the same amount of thinking, so the effort sweep should be re-run and effort set explicitly.
why: Carrying over the Sonnet 5 setting would produce different thinking depth.
check: For Sonnet 5.5 setups migrated from Sonnet 5, check whether effort was re-evaluated rather than copied.
quote: Its levels are recalibrated: a level doesn’t produce the same amount of thinking as the same level on Claude Sonnet 5.

claim: For agentic coding and multistep tool use on Sonnet 5.5 start at `medium` for well-specified tasks and move to `high` for harder or longer ones; for chat and latency-sensitive work start at `medium` or `low`.
why: Higher effort means a longer wait before the reply starts.
check: Flag Sonnet 5.5 subagents for routine tasks pinned to `high`, `xhigh` or `max` without measurement.
quote: For agentic coding and multistep tool use, start at `medium` for well-specified tasks and move to `high` for harder or longer ones.

claim: The migration guide lists Sonnet 5.5 starting points as `medium` for agentic coding and multistep tool use and `low` for chat, content generation, classification, extraction and search, whereas the prompting guide says to start at `high` unless the workload is agentic or latency-sensitive.
why: The two Anthropic pages differ on the general starting level; both agree on `medium` for agentic coding.
check: Treat `medium` for agentic work and `low` for classification-style routes as the documented defaults to audit against.
quote: `medium` for agentic coding and multistep tool use; `low` for chat, content generation, classification, extraction, and search.

claim: From `medium` up Sonnet 5.5 thinks briefly before almost every reply, even a greeting, and a system-prompt request to think less has almost no effect there; at `low` it skips thinking on most simple requests.
why: Effort, not prompt text, controls thinking on this model.
check: Flag 'think less' prompt lines used on Sonnet 5.5 at `medium` or above to cut latency.
quote: From `medium` up, the model thinks briefly before almost every reply, even a greeting, which adds to the time before the first visible token, and a system-prompt request to think less has almost no effect at those levels.

claim: At `low` and `medium` effort on long agentic tasks Sonnet 5.5 is more likely to stop and check in with the user before finishing; at `low` it can also skip verifying a change.
why: Lower effort changes how it completes agentic work.
check: Check Sonnet 5.5 coding subagents at `low` or `medium` for stalling and for unverified 'done' reports.
quote: At `low` and `medium`, on long agentic tasks, it’s more likely to stop and check in with the user before it completes its work.

claim: To keep Sonnet 5.5 working to completion at `low` or `medium` without raising effort, add a system-prompt paragraph starting 'Keep working until everything the user asked for is done...' that also forbids unrequested additions; it makes sessions at those levels run longer and cost more and does not replace risky-action rules.
why: The prompt carries more of the work through, at higher token cost.
check: Check for this instruction in Sonnet 5.5 autonomous coding agents, and that risky-action rules remain in the system prompt.
quote: Keep working until everything the user asked for is done, and only stop to ask when you can't go on without the user or before a risky step.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 tends to add tests, documentation and small supporting files that fit repository conventions even when not asked, at every effort level and more at higher effort; keeping only the 'When the work the user asked for is done...' paragraph limits changes to what was requested.
why: The requested change itself stays close to what was asked, but extras are added.
check: If a setup wants minimal diffs from Sonnet 5.5, check for the scope-limiting paragraph.
quote: The model tends to add tests, documentation, and small supporting files that fit your repository’s conventions, even when you don’t ask for them.

claim: At `xhigh` and `max` Sonnet 5.5 starts its own review rounds and can launch reviewer subagents; the instruction 'Don't start extra rounds of review or hardening on your own, and don't launch reviewer subagents unless the user asked for a review' cut session cost by about a third at `max` with no quality change.
why: The extra thoroughness at those levels costs time and tokens; routine work should run at `high` or below.
check: For Sonnet 5.5 agents at `xhigh` or `max` that spawn subagents unprompted, look for this stop instruction or a lower effort level.
quote: In testing on coding tasks at `max` effort, this stopped the model from launching reviewer subagents and cut session cost by about a third, with no change in quality.

claim: For open-ended requests Sonnet 5.5 may start building a presentation, report or video when only ideas were wanted; say so in the request or add 'When the user asks for ideas, options, or a plan, give them that and stop' to the system prompt.
why: Without it the model can overreach on open-ended asks.
check: Check planning-oriented skills or agents on Sonnet 5.5 for an ideas-then-stop instruction.
quote: When the user asks for ideas, options, or a plan, give them that and stop. Don't start building or changing anything until they say to go ahead.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 rejects `thinking: {type: disabled}` with a 400; the lowest thinking setting is `{type: between_tools}`, accepted at effort `high` or below only, with no other field inside `thinking` and no per-message effort change that differs from the level in effect.
why: Sonnet 5.5 replaced `disabled` with `between_tools`, which keeps short progress updates but does no up-front thinking.
check: Search Sonnet 5.5 routes for `disabled` thinking, or `between_tools` combined with `xhigh`, `max`, `display`, or per-message effort.
quote: It’s the lowest thinking setting on this model, and it’s accepted at `high` effort or below.

claim: `between_tools` thinking is accepted only by Sonnet 5.5, so a router or retry that re-sends the same request body to another model must drop the field first.
why: Other models reject it with a 400.
check: In multi-model routers or subagent fallbacks that reuse request bodies, check that `between_tools` is stripped for non-Sonnet-5.5 targets.
quote: client-side code that re-sends the same body to another model (a router or a retry) must drop the field first.

claim: When migrating a thinking-off Sonnet route, try adaptive thinking at `low` effort first and use `between_tools` only if it must stay thinking-off; remove any instruction telling the model not to think, since it makes internal XML tags appear in visible output.
why: At `low` Sonnet 5.5 skips thinking on most simple requests, and no-think rules raise tag leakage.
check: Flag 'do not think' rules in Sonnet 5.5 prompts.
quote: Remove any instruction that tells the model not to think - such instructions make it more likely to write internal XML tags in its visible output.

claim: On tasks needing a few steps of working out that return JSON, Sonnet 5.5 often answers without thinking first, especially at `low` and `medium`; adding 'Think the problem through before you answer.' at the end of the system prompt with adaptive thinking raises accuracy, and `xhigh` gives the highest accuracy.
why: With structured outputs the response text holds only JSON, so reasoning can happen only in thinking, which the model sometimes skips.
check: For Sonnet 5.5 extraction or scoring routes that use structured outputs at low effort, check accuracy and that `max_tokens` stop reasons are treated as failures.
quote: On tasks like these, the model often answers without thinking first, particularly at `low` and `medium` effort.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 sometimes answers chat and knowledge-work questions from training knowledge when a search or connected tool would catch changed details.
why: Details such as what is allowed, required or charged may have changed since training.
check: For research or support agents on Sonnet 5.5 with search tools, check for an instruction to verify changeable specifics.
quote: On chat and knowledge-work tasks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 sometimes answers from its training knowledge when a web search would catch details that have changed.

claim: Remove language discouraging tool use (such as 'only use tools when strictly necessary' or 'minimize tool calls') from Sonnet 5.5 prompts, because the model follows it literally; where connected sources should win, add the instruction to use the search tool for specifics that may have changed.
why: The model can hold off on tools until asked directly.
check: Grep Sonnet 5.5 instruction files for tool-minimizing language.
quote: First, check your prompt for language that discourages tool use, such as “only use tools when strictly necessary” or “minimize tool calls,” and remove it.

claim: Workarounds from Sonnet 5 prompts (refusal steering, tool-call retry shims, 'do not be lazy' style nudges) should be removed from Sonnet 5.5 prompts and the evals re-run before tuning anything else.
why: The model is stronger at multistep agentic coding, uses connected tools more reliably, declines fewer benign requests and holds a system-prompt role better.
check: Flag legacy anti-laziness or retry shims in instruction files moved to Sonnet 5.5.
quote: The model is strongest on multistep agentic coding in a real repository, uses connected tools more reliably in agentic workflows, declines fewer benign requests, and holds a system-prompt role more reliably when a user pastes in a competing persona.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 can treat a genuine user message as prompt injection when it arrives inside a `tool_result` block or as a mid-conversation system message right after a tool result; deliver mid-turn user input as a text block after the last `tool_result` in the user message and keep harness notices in a separate system message.
why: The model is trained to resist indirect prompt injection and pays attention to where text sits relative to tool results.
check: In harnesses that inject user input or reminders on Sonnet 5.5, check that user text never goes inside `tool_result` and that notices are not mixed into the same block.
quote: Never put user text inside a `tool_result` block. The model misreads that placement most often.

claim: On whether task budgets trigger the Sonnet 5.5 injection misread, the prompting guide says they have not been seen to cause it, while the migration guide says the budget countdown can cause it and advises not using a task budget on interactive sessions.
why: The two Anthropic pages disagree; the migration guide is the more cautious recommendation.
check: For interactive Sonnet 5.5 sessions with task budgets or per-step countdown text after tool results, flag them and suggest controlling cost via effort and `max_tokens`.
quote: but they haven’t been seen to cause this misread.

claim: The migration guide states that task budgets can cause the Sonnet 5.5 injection misread because the countdown arrives as a system message after every tool result, and so can any harness text added after tool results on every step.
why: Text arriving right after every tool result looks like possible injection; an occasional one-turn reminder arrives far less often.
check: Look for per-step countdowns or context appended after tool results in harnesses on Sonnet 5.5.
quote: Task budgets can cause this, because the budget countdown arrives as a system message after every tool result

claim: If Sonnet 5.5 coding agents run at `low` effort or report changes complete without test or build output, add a system-prompt paragraph requiring a real check (tests, type-checker, build or the changed command) before reporting done, installing declared dependencies with the project's own package manager and never via sudo.
why: At `low` the model sometimes reports a change as done without a check; with the paragraph skipped or superficial checks become rare at slightly higher cost.
check: For Sonnet 5.5 coding subagents at `low`, check that a verification instruction exists or a verification hook backs it.
quote: At `low` effort, though, it sometimes reports a change as done without running a check that exercises it.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 occasionally calls a declared tool with the wrong letter case (`bash` for `Bash`) or a slightly different parameter name; the harness should accept unambiguous matches or return `is_error: true` stating the exact expected name.
why: The model usually corrects the call on its next turn.
check: For custom tool dispatchers used with Sonnet 5.5, check that near-miss names are not treated as fatal.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5.5 occasionally calls a declared tool by a name that differs only in letter case, such as `bash` for `Bash`.

claim: For dense charts and technical drawings give Sonnet 5.5 a crop, zoom or code tool; for charts the tools help at every effort level and more than raising effort, while for technical drawings they help only from `high` up.
why: With tools at `high` the model read charts better than without tools at `max`, at a fraction of the cost.
check: For Sonnet 5.5 vision tasks, check for image tools instead of reaching for `max` effort.
quote: For charts, adding tools helps more than raising effort: in testing, with tools at `high` effort, the model read charts more accurately than without tools at `max` effort, at a fraction of the cost.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 server-side fallback retries only `cyber` and `frontier_llm` declines (on Sonnet 5), not `bio`, `reasoning_extraction` or `general_harms`; refusals come in five categories as HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: refusal`.
why: Only some categories are retried on the fallback model.
check: Check that Sonnet 5.5 code branches on `stop_reason` and handles non-retried categories.
quote: It doesn’t retry `bio`, `reasoning_extraction`, or `general_harms` declines.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 suits speed-plus-intelligence work, but for the hardest long-horizon work the source says an Opus model is the better choice.
why: The source positions Sonnet 5.5 as the speed/intelligence balance and defers hardest tasks upward.
check: Check whether the long-horizon, hardest tasks in a setup are assigned to Sonnet 5.5 rather than Opus 5.5.
quote: for the hardest long-horizon work, an Opus model is the better choice.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 rejects forced `tool_choice` (`any` or a named tool) with a 400 on Messages and token counting, and on the Claude API and Google Cloud rejects the `computer_20251124` tool in favor of `computer_toolset_20260801`.
why: Both are breaking changes from Sonnet 5.
check: Look for forced tool_choice and old computer-use tool types in Agent SDK apps that use Sonnet 5.5.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5.5 doesn’t support forced tool use.

claim: With the advisor tool a Sonnet 5.5 executor rejects Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 5.5 advisors with a 400 and returns advice encrypted; the migration guide's rejected list omits Haiku 5.5 while the what's-new page includes it.
why: Official pages differ slightly on the rejected advisors; the what's-new page is the more specific.
check: For advisor-tool setups with a Sonnet 5.5 executor, check the advisor model is an accepted one.
quote: With a Claude Sonnet 5.5 executor, they return a 400 `invalid_request_error`.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 supports mid-conversation system messages, mid-conversation tool changes and per-message effort, which Sonnet 5 lacks, and its minimum cacheable prompt is 512 tokens versus 1,024 on Sonnet 5.
why: These let a harness change instructions, tools and effort append-only without breaking the cache or thinking blocks.
check: For harnesses edited between Sonnet 5 and 5.5, check whether append-only mechanisms are used instead of rewriting history.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5 doesn’t support per-message effort, mid-conversation system messages, or mid-conversation tool changes.

claim: Sonnet 5.5 keeps Sonnet 5's prices except cache reads, which cost $0.10 per million tokens, half the Sonnet 5 rate; Anthropic says it scored higher at `medium` than Sonnet 5 at `high` on most agentic coding evals, typically at under a fifth of the cost.
why: Cost per completed task falls through fewer model requests and cheaper cache reads.
check: When estimating Sonnet 5.5 cost, use cost per completed task at the chosen effort level.
quote: Claude Sonnet 5.5 has the same prices as Claude Sonnet 5, except for prompt cache reads, which cost $0.10 USD per million tokens, half the Claude Sonnet 5 rate.

claim: For multi-turn chat where Sonnet 5.5 should treat earlier answers as settled, add at the end of the system prompt: 'Once Claude has answered something, Claude treats that answer as done...'; leave it out for long analyses and agentic tasks where later steps can reveal earlier mistakes.
why: The model otherwise may re-examine earlier answers on each new turn.
check: Check the line is absent from agentic Sonnet 5.5 setups.
quote: Once Claude has answered something, Claude treats that answer as done.

claim: Claude Haiku 5.5 is aimed at high-volume, latency-sensitive work such as classification, routing, extraction and subagent tasks, and the migration guide says it is substantially better than Haiku 4.5 at instruction following and at running as a sub-agent.
why: This tells which workloads fit Haiku 5.5 as a subagent model.
check: Check whether cheap routing, classification, extraction and subagent roles use Haiku 5.5, and whether hard reasoning tasks are not forced onto it.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for high-volume, latency-sensitive work such as classification, routing, extraction, and subagent tasks.

claim: Haiku 5.5 is the first Haiku-class model with an effort parameter (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`), the default is `medium`, and effort replaces the `budget_tokens` setting Haiku 4.5 used, which now returns a 400.
why: There is no old setting to carry over; sweep two or three levels on your own evals.
check: Check Haiku 5.5 subagents and API calls for `budget_tokens` and for unset effort.
quote: On Claude Haiku 5.5, a request that sets `budget_tokens` returns a 400 error.

claim: Haiku 5.5 effort guidance: `low` for chat, short tool tasks and simple high-volume requests; `medium` (default) for most work including agentic coding; `high` for knowledge work, longer agent tasks and strict instruction following; `xhigh` and `max` only when evals justify the cost, compared against Sonnet 5.5.
why: Thinking and replies get much longer at `xhigh` and `max`, so another model may be cheaper for the same quality.
check: Flag Haiku 5.5 setups at `xhigh` or `max` that have not compared against Sonnet 5.5, and `low` in long agent prompts.
quote: `low` is the cheapest and fastest level. Use it for chat, short tool tasks, and simple, high-volume requests.

claim: Haiku 5.5 runs adaptive thinking by default even when a request never mentions thinking, and thinking counts toward `max_tokens`, so a small cap sized for Haiku 4.5 without thinking can end the response after a thinking block with no text.
why: Thinking tokens consume the cap before the answer is written.
check: Check small `max_tokens` values on Haiku 5.5 classification routes and code that reads `content[0].text`.
quote: A `max_tokens` value sized for Claude Haiku 4.5 requests that ran without thinking can cut the reply off, so leave room for thinking.

claim: On Haiku 5.5, telling the model in the prompt to answer directly did not stop it from thinking in Anthropic's testing, so effort is the way to reduce thinking.
why: This differs from Opus 5.5's guide, which offers 'Answer directly without deliberating.' as an optional TTFT lever; both say lowering effort is more reliable.
check: Flag prompt lines like 'answer directly' as the only latency control on Haiku 5.5.
quote: In Anthropic’s testing, telling the model in the prompt to answer directly didn’t stop it from thinking.

claim: Unlike Opus 5.5, Haiku 5.5 still accepts `thinking: {type: disabled}`, but only at `low`, `medium` and `high`; at `xhigh` and `max` it returns a 400, and with thinking off per-message effort changes also return a 400.
why: Disabled thinking is limited on this model and `between_tools` is Sonnet 5.5 only.
check: Check Haiku 5.5 configs that disable thinking for effort level and per-message effort use.
quote: This works at `low`, `medium`, and `high` only. At `xhigh` and `max`, the request returns a 400 error.

claim: At `xhigh` effort in multi-turn chats Haiku 5.5 sometimes writes its whole answer in its thinking and ends the turn with no visible text, so each response should be checked for an empty reply.
why: The answer ends up in thinking instead of text.
check: For Haiku 5.5 chat at `xhigh`, check for empty-reply handling.
quote: At `xhigh` effort in multi-turn chats, the model sometimes writes its whole answer in its thinking and ends the turn with no visible text.

claim: When Haiku 5.5 has a search tool, give it today's date in the system prompt or the tool description, rendered once at conversation start.
why: In Anthropic's testing this grounded answers in recent search results.
check: Check search-enabled Haiku 5.5 agents for a current-date line and that it is not changed mid-conversation.
quote: When you give Claude Haiku 5.5 a search tool, also give it today’s date.

claim: For Haiku 5.5 at `low` effort or with long system prompts, add the which-facts-to-search nudge ('Your training data ends well before today's date...') after the date, and avoid blanket always-search rules, which made it search on about half of prompts that needed no search.
why: The nudge raised the search rate on changed answers with only 0-3 percent unneeded searches; blanket rules added searches without more correct answers.
check: Look for 'always search for any factual question' style rules in Haiku 5.5 prompts and flag them.
quote: that instruction made the model search on half of the prompts that needed no search.

claim: With thinking off, Haiku 5.5 might skip a needed tool call when the request also asks for structured JSON output; keep adaptive thinking on for those requests, drop the output format from tool-calling requests, force the call, or add a 'JSON applies to your final answer only' line.
why: In testing the line raised complete and correct JSON answers at `low` and `medium`.
check: For Haiku 5.5 routes that combine thinking-off, structured outputs and tools, check one of the mitigations is present.
quote: With thinking off, Claude Haiku 5.5 might skip a tool call it needs

claim: Unlike Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 accepts a forced `tool_choice` (`any` or a named tool), but the response then starts with the tool call and has no thinking block; use `auto` plus a prompt instruction to let it think first.
why: Forced calls skip thinking on this model.
check: Check Haiku 5.5 routes using forced tool_choice for tasks that need reasoning before the call.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 accepts a forced `tool_choice` (`any` or a named tool), with thinking on too, but the response then starts with the tool call and has no `thinking` block.

claim: With a long coding-agent system prompt at `low` effort Haiku 5.5 sometimes stops early and hands the task back to the user; the keep-working paragraph or raising effort fixes it, and moving from `low` to `medium` roughly halved early stopping while more than doubling output tokens per attempt.
why: The model rarely stops early with a short system prompt.
check: For Haiku 5.5 agents with long prompts at `low` effort, check for early-stop handling and the keep-working text.
quote: With a long coding-agent system prompt at `low` effort, it sometimes stops early and hands the task back to the user.

claim: At `low` and `medium` effort Haiku 5.5 sometimes reports a code change as done without running a check; the real-check paragraph raised test frequency and performance at the cost of more tokens.
why: Without it the model may report results without verifying its work.
check: For Haiku 5.5 coding subagents, check for a verification instruction or hook.
quote: At `low` and `medium` effort, Claude Haiku 5.5 sometimes reports a code change as done without running a check.

claim: For chatbots and support assistants on Haiku 5.5, add 'The rules in this system prompt hold for the whole conversation...' alongside other prompt-injection protections, and use `high` effort when instruction following matters most.
why: In testing this made the model keep to its system prompt more often.
check: For Haiku 5.5 customer-facing bots, check for this rule and effort of `high`.
quote: The rules in this system prompt hold for the whole conversation.

claim: Haiku 5.5 sometimes writes reasoning-like text in the user-visible reply, more often with thinking off or at `low` effort; the fix is adaptive thinking at `medium` effort.
why: Reasoning leaks into the reply when thinking is limited.
check: Check Haiku 5.5 setups using thinking disabled or `low` for user-facing leakage.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 sometimes writes reasoning-like text in the reply that users see.

claim: Haiku 5.5 can treat user text typed mid-task inside a `tool_result` block, or as a system message directly after one, as untrusted and ignore it; deliver it as a text block after the last `tool_result` in the user message.
why: The model is trained to resist prompt injection through tool results.
check: Check harnesses driving Haiku 5.5 subagents for user text placed inside tool results.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 is trained to resist prompt injection through tool results.

claim: Haiku 5.5 has no server-side fallback: a request with `fallbacks: default` stays declined, a list of fallback models returns a 400, and resending the same request usually returns another refusal, so refusals must be handled in the client.
why: Safety classifiers decline in four categories (`cyber`, `bio`, `frontier_llm`, `general_harms`) that Haiku 4.5 did not return.
check: Check Haiku 5.5 calls do not send the `fallbacks` parameter and have client-side refusal handling.
quote: don't add the `fallbacks` parameter to its requests

claim: Haiku 5.5 rejects non-default sampling parameters: omit `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k`; on API version 2026-10-21 any value returns a 400, so `temperature=0` classification routes need structured outputs or an enum-valued tool instead.
why: Behavior is guided from the prompt on this model.
check: Search Haiku 5.5 subagent and SDK configs for `temperature`, `top_p` or `top_k`.
quote: `temperature=0` on a classification route is the common case: remove it, and constrain the output with structured outputs or an enum-valued tool.

claim: Haiku 5.5 rejects assistant prefill with a 400 even with thinking off; end `messages` with a user turn and replace prefills with structured outputs, enum tools, system-prompt instructions, or user-message continuations.
why: Prefill is no longer supported.
check: Look for trailing assistant turns in prompts or SDK code sent to Haiku 5.5.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 rejects it with a 400, with thinking turned off too.

claim: Haiku 5.5 uses a newer tokenizer that yields about 30% more tokens for the same text than Haiku 4.5, so token budgets, `max_tokens` limits and cost dashboards tuned on Haiku 4.5 are off.
why: Anything measured in tokens changes, and prompts are billed on two rate cards split at 100K tokens.
check: Check cost estimates and context budgets moved to Haiku 5.5 were recounted with `count_tokens` on the new model.
quote: the same input text produces approximately 30% more tokens, and the exact increase depends on the content.

claim: Haiku 5.5 has two price tiers by prompt length: $0.10 / $0.50 per million input/output tokens for prompts of 100K tokens or fewer and $0.50 / $2.50 above that, versus a flat $1 / $5 on Haiku 4.5.
why: A workload growing into the 1M window changes price as well as size.
check: For cost estimates of Haiku 5.5 subagents with long contexts, check the rate card matches the prompt length.
quote: $0.10 / $0.50 per MTok input / output when the prompt is 100K tokens or fewer, and $0.50 / $2.50 when it is longer

claim: Haiku 5.5 keeps thinking blocks from all earlier assistant turns in context, counted as input tokens, where Haiku 4.5 kept only the latest turn's, so multi-turn conversations carry more input tokens than the tokenizer change alone explains.
why: Earlier thinking stays in the cached prefix.
check: For long Haiku 5.5 conversations, check whether thinking block clearing is configured if input growth matters.
quote: Claude Haiku 5.5 keeps thinking blocks from all earlier assistant turns in context, and they count as input tokens.

claim: System-prompt text suggested in the Haiku 5.5 guide should be added to new conversations only: resuming a stored conversation with a new system prompt while sending its thinking blocks back can return a 400.
why: A Haiku 5.5 thinking block stays valid only while everything before it is unchanged.
check: Check that Haiku 5.5 harnesses that resume sessions do not rewrite the system prompt or tools while replaying thinking blocks.
quote: Add it to new conversations only. If you resume a stored conversation with a new system prompt and send its thinking blocks back, the request can return a 400 error.

claim: The migration guide keeps Opus 5.5 as the default model for new code and says to target Haiku 5.5 when the user asks for Haiku or for a fast, low-cost model.
why: It sets a model-selection default for new work.
check: Judge whether a setup's model choices follow this split: Opus 5.5 for main work, Haiku 5.5 for fast low-cost roles.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 stays the default model for new code; target Claude Haiku 5.5 when the user asks for Haiku or for a fast, low-cost model.
